title: Tuesday, November 3: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen, and two more
description:
The three biggest Hacker News stories for Tuesday, November 3.

1. Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
   Article: https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/
   Discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50341174

2. WTF Ubuntu?
   Article: https://chalmovsky.com/posts/wtf-ubuntu
   Discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50337608

3. Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
   Discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50340088

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Can an AI model look at the raw numbers inside another neural network and tell you what it does? One lab says yes, and it used that trick to make a small open model far better at math, without any training. I'm Maya, and this is Upvoted, the top of Hacker News for Tuesday, November 3. A critical Linux bug that Debian patched weeks ago is still open on Ubuntu. And a pair of glasses that hears you without you making a sound. Stick around. Three stories, about twelve minutes, and you're caught up.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The top story on Hacker News this morning, with about twenty-nine hundred points, is a blog post called Weight-Space Programming. Its claim is that a model called GPT-6 Astra can read the weights of a neural network, the raw numbers it learned in training, and work out what that network does. Then change it. Theo has been following this. Good morning.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Good morning, Maya.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Start with the reading part. What did they actually show?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: They handed Astra about seventeen thousand weights from a tiny network trained to play a video game. No tools, no way to run it. Just the numbers. And it answered Breakout, ninety-nine percent confident. That's the party trick.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the part that got people's attention?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: They asked it to make Qwen three point five, a small open model, better at math, again with no training. Astra noticed the model kept getting stuck in reasoning loops. Eighty-five of its first ninety-six practice answers just ran until they hit the length limit. It traced that to one direction in two of the model's layers and subtracted it out.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the result?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: It touched a tiny fraction of a percent of the weights, and the math score went from about eight percent to forty-eight.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's a big jump. How is the Hacker News crowd taking it?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: With some caution. One commenter who says they do research in weight-space learning urged people to read the paper first. Their view is that the write-up oversells it, that Qwen already knew the math and was simply un-stuck. Others pointed out that removing a direction that causes looping was already a known technique, and one person said their master's thesis back in twenty eighteen was on predicting weights.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Has anyone tried it themselves?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: A couple of people, with mixed results. One tried the same approach on a small model that turns plain English into shell commands. It fixed some mistakes and introduced others, no net gain. But another commenter ran the same prompts on a Qwen model on their own laptop, and it named Pac-Man, Breakout and Pong. It only missed Freeway.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So where does that leave it?

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Probably not magic. But a lot of readers say they upvoted because they hadn't realized this was possible at all, and they want to see what happens as these models get bigger.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's Theo. Thanks.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, a Linux security story with a blunt headline, which I'll paraphrase as: what on earth, Ubuntu? It's about a bug in the Linux kernel's networking code, rated nine point eight out of ten on the CVSS severity scale. The author's complaint is less about the bug than about how long Ubuntu has taken to fix it. Nadia has been following this one. Good morning.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Good morning, Maya.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Nadia, how serious is this bug?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: On paper, about as serious as they come. It's been in the kernel since twenty sixteen, and it can be reached remotely. Anthropic says it built a working exploit that gets full control of a server.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the complaint about Ubuntu?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Debian shipped a fix on October sixteenth. The author says that more than two weeks later, every supported Ubuntu release was still listed as vulnerable, long-term support releases included. They point out that volunteer-run distributions shipped the fix while Canonical, which sells security subscriptions, hadn't. They took their Ubuntu servers offline and say they're moving off for good.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Is the danger as high as that score suggests?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: That's the real debate in the thread. One commenter noted the predicted chance of exploitation is under one percent, and that most advisories describe a crash, not a takeover. Anthropic is the main source for the claim that it gets you full control. Ubuntu's own page rates it high priority, not critical.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Has Canonical responded?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Someone from Canonical's product team did, in the thread. They said fixes for twenty-two oh four and newer are in the proposed pocket, being tested for stability, and that the company has published a blog post with details. The replies weren't sympathetic. The most common one was that three weeks is plenty of time.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Anyone defending the wait?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: A few. One person warned that one of those proposed kernels has serious regressions, so rushing has its own cost. And another thought the post was more outrage than detail. But many agreed that a company charging for security gets held to a higher bar.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's Nadia. Thank you.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Thanks, Maya.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Finally, a Show H N, where people post something they've built. Two founders, Aarush and Arnav, have made smart glasses that let you talk to your computer silently. You mouth the words, and the glasses turn them into text. Felix has been following this. Good morning.

lines.speaker: Felix
lines.text: Good morning, Maya.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: How do glasses read words nobody says out loud?

lines.speaker: Felix
lines.text: They send out radio waves, a bit like Bluetooth, that pass through your face. Your tongue and lips change the signal as you mouth words, and the founders' models decode that into text.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Where did the idea come from?

lines.speaker: Felix
lines.text: They were computer science students at Georgia Tech. At a hackathon, they tried it with electrodes stuck on one founder's face. That ran into sweat and interference, and, in their words, nobody wants electrodes on their face. So they switched to radio. To make it work for different people, they paid volunteers to sit in booths and read prompts while wearing the glasses.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Do people really want to talk to their computers instead of typing?

lines.speaker: Felix
lines.text: One commenter asked exactly that, saying they read aloud more slowly than they think. The founder answered that most people type forty to fifty words a minute and talk at a hundred twenty to two hundred.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And privacy? This is something reading your mouth all day.

lines.speaker: Felix
lines.text: That came up a lot. Some people said they'd only use it if it ran fully offline. Right now, the founder said, the decoding happens in the cloud, through a companion app.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Who seemed most excited?

lines.speaker: Felix
lines.text: People who find typing or speaking hard. One commenter scheduled for carpal tunnel surgery on both hands said it's exactly what they've been looking for. Another pointed out it could help people with tracheostomies, who can move their mouths but can't use their voice. And one asked the founders to keep adjustable nose pads, because they have a big nose. The founder said yes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: When can people get one?

lines.speaker: Felix
lines.text: They're aiming to ship in the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's Felix. Thanks.

lines.speaker: Felix
lines.text: Thank you, Maya.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And that's Upvoted for this Tuesday, November 3. I'm Maya. Our correspondents were Theo, Nadia and Felix. Upvoted is written by Claude and voiced by Gemini, and links to every story are in the show notes. We'll have the top of Hacker News for you again tomorrow morning.
